name: Sara Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Sara, 43, and I lead developers building online exam software for a tech company. I have a master’s degree and I’m good at finding why an answer was saved late or a timed question vanished. I start with school reports, review code and test a fix with a proctor before release. I use AI every day for test drafts and log searches, then check the student’s actual session record myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does your job support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Niko, coaches youth sports, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My developer pay is high, and we have about nine months of expenses saved. There are plenty of similar jobs nearby. Niko’s coaching hours move with the season, so my wage pays the mortgage most months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau is close to the assistant I already use: quick drafts, with people checking the exam session. A student should not lose a mark to a tidy-looking log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would feel secure about work and our bills. Nine months saved can carry us through a slow sports season while my job holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep drafting tests with AI and compare each answer-save alert with the student’s session. I’d continue transferring 600 into savings monthly while my pay holds. In the first year I’d ask proctors to sign off on fixes to lost-answer cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my income. I still feel for a student who watches an answer disappear, but I do not see a job cut here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which lost answer stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One student’s essay looked blank after a network pause although the text was saved. I found the saved version and had the proctor confirm it before grades closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family budget change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Niko we can keep the children’s holiday camp and still save. I would not spend the reserve on a larger home just because one year went well.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking student sessions.
I would keep **proctor sign-off** on lost-answer fixes.
think: I expect my **lead job and pay** to remain secure while people check exams.
Our **nine-month reserve** covers slow coaching seasons and current mortgage bills.
do: **Keep** drafting AI tests and checking actual exam sessions.
**Transfer** 600 monthly into savings while developer pay holds.
feel: **Calm** about bills, with concern for affected students.
S0.quote: A student should not lose a mark to a tidy-looking log.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** is checked against student sessions and proctor confirmation.
High pay, **nine months saved** and many nearby jobs make the mild world secure for her.

steps.text: Keep testing exam answers against actual student session records
Transfer 600 monthly into savings while developer pay holds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let AI write code, grade routine items and answer students faster. I would ask schools to test changes before management lowers the human review time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my lead role may remain while junior hiring slows. Niko’s coaching work is hands-on, but booking and schedules could still move to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d use our AI assistant to replay twenty old answer-loss cases and compare what it reports with each student’s saved work. I’d ask a school proctor to mark any missed harm, then propose an automated flag only if management approves and all cases pass. In the first year I’d attend the local developers’ association if junior hiring freezes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own wage looks safe for now, but I do not want junior work to vanish or a student’s appeal to become a chatbot loop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a junior developer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would give a junior colleague the network-pause case and ask them to find the saved essay. Learning where the evidence sits matters more than a fast draft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Niko change his booking system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Niko how many paid coaching places come through online booking before we change his system. We would not buy new software because a vendor promises full classes.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed code, routine grading and replies.
I would require **school-tested changes** before review time falls.
think: I expect my **lead wage** to hold while junior hiring slows.
I worry **coaching bookings** may change before hands-on lessons.
do: **Replay** twenty old answer-loss cases with AI and proctor review.
**Enable** an automatic loss flag only if management approves and all cases pass.
**Attend** the developers’ association if junior hiring freezes.
feel: **Uneasy** about entry jobs and student appeals, with my pay secure.
S1.quote: Learning where the evidence sits matters more than a fast draft.
fieldNote: She uses **AI daily** and adds an approved flag only after student-record and proctor checks.
Her **association action** depends on a hiring freeze, while her own income looks safe.

steps.text: Enable AI answer-loss flag only after management approval and twenty checked cases
Attend developers association if junior hiring freezes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches exam-code thinking work in 2028. Hands-on robots arrive around 2031, so Niko’s coaching sessions may have more time than my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the company could cut most coding roles, including mine. Nine months saved gives us time, but other local developer jobs could shrink together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d delay the deposit on a larger home and keep that cash available. I’d ask the company for written severance and paid transition terms, then check actual vacancies rather than assume schools will need programmers. In the first year after 2028, if laid off, I’d apply to real openings and seek income help only if eligible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own job, though I can act with nine months of savings. A bigger house would turn one lost wage into a larger mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about a bigger house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children the current bedrooms still work and we can wait. I would not sign a larger loan until income is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain for exam appeals?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a proctor whether paid appeals work still exists before paying for another qualification. I would not use the mortgage reserve for a course brochure.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach exam code before hands-on robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues **coaching sessions** may change later.
think: I expect **major coding cuts** could include me even with a strong work record.
Our **nine-month savings** cannot guarantee another software job if firms shrink together.
do: **Delay** moving to a larger home and keep its deposit in cash.
**Request** written severance and paid transition terms.
**Apply** for actual openings and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost pay, with nine months to plan.
S2.quote: A bigger house would turn one lost wage into a larger mortgage.
fieldNote: She faces the **2028 code shock** before robots around 2031 might affect hands-on coaching.
The **home move** is delayed; new jobs and public help remain conditional, with no course bought on speculation.

steps.text: Delay moving to larger home and hold its deposit for mortgage
Apply for actual local openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to learn how students contest lost marks. Thinking AI reaches exam code in 2031; hands-on robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect fewer coding jobs, but I could test whether schools pay for careful exam audits. I cannot assume appeals work stays paid after full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d offer two schools a six-month pilot of independent answer-loss audits, using only records they approve and only if my employer clears the outside work in writing. I’d charge a fixed fee for each accepted report and stop if fees do not cover travel, secure storage and childcare. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d continue only if paid repeat work covers those costs and family time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about code pay, but I can test demand without borrowing against our home. The schools may decline the pilot entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a real audit customer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count accepted paid reports, not friendly meetings. If neither school signs a data agreement, there is no audit business to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who covers the children and student data?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Niko would cover the children on audit days only if his coaching timetable allows. I would cancel a visit rather than use student records without permission.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to test paid exam audits.
I know **2034 robots** follow the earlier code shock.
think: I expect **fewer coding jobs** despite warning.
I cannot assume **appeals audits** stay paid after full thinking AI.
do: **Pilot six-month audits** at two schools only with approved records and written employer clearance.
**Charge** for accepted reports; stop if fees miss travel, storage and childcare costs.
**Continue** after 2031 coding loss only if paid repeat reports cover costs and family time.
feel: **Anxious** about coding pay, with a limited paid-demand test.
S3.quote: If neither school signs a data agreement, there is no audit business to build.
fieldNote: Her **two-school pilot** requires school consent, secure records and written clearance from her employer.
The **fee gate** covers travel, secure storage, childcare and family time; Niko’s timetable matters.

steps.text: Pilot six-month two-school audits only with data consent, written employer clearance and Niko’s childcare
Charge per accepted report; stop pilot if fees fail travel, storage and childcare costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to make exam systems easier to audit. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my pay to hold for now, and the family reserve gives us options. I would still watch for the company using AI as a reason to stop hiring new developers today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking exam sessions against saved answers and save 600 monthly while my pay holds. I’d ask the developers’ association to publish junior hiring and paid training figures each year. In the first year after 2036, if coding ends, I’d search actual local openings before changing the children’s school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long view, though the mortgage is secure now. A decade gives us time to measure whether anyone new gets a chance to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the association report count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the association to name the jobs that were filled, not just count training sessions. A lesson with no paid role afterward is not the same as an opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Niko and I would keep the current home unless a real offer covers another mortgage and the children’s travel. We would not move on a prediction.

I know **2039 robots** follow the earlier code shift.

I worry **junior hiring** may slow before 2036.

fieldNote: She uses the **long warning** to press for measured hiring and funded learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because exam-code work could vanish before we know what coaching remains. Written severance, paid transition time and real openings would help. I might test paid audit work later, but a friendly school meeting is not income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tells a student that a saved answer was lost after the exam closed. A blank screen can erase a mark without erasing the work.

headlineQuote: A blank screen can erase a mark without erasing the work.
portrait: Sara is a **43-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree, high pay and nine months of expenses saved.
She uses **AI daily** in exam software, checking suggestions against actual student sessions and proctors.
Her partner’s **coaching hours** vary; hands-on lessons face robots later than her code.
She tests **paid exam audits** only with school data consent, employer clearance, childcare and accepted fees.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her coding role despite a strong savings reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid transition time and real openings would help.
